1) network monitoring is a natural fit for streaming analytics, 2) it is important to be able to express queries in terms of tuples, and 3) it is possible to partition network monitoring queries across both the switches (for filtering) and the stream processor (for fusion) so as to enable streaming analytics to scale to very large traffic volumes.

network monitoring is an important application for streaming analytics and that it is possible to build a closed-loop system, such as Sonata, to perform streaming analytics on traffic streams at high rates.
network monitoring queries can be expressed as streaming queries, and that iterative and adaptive filtering can be used to scale network monitoring queries to high data rates.

how to make network monitoring queries scalable to traffic rates that are orders of magnitude higher than today's traffic rates, and we believe that Sonata is a step in the right direction.

we show that it is possible for operators to perform streaming analysis on the network, at high rates, by using programmable switches and stream processors in conjunction with a runtime system that iteratively refines the query and extracts only the traffic that is pertinent to the query.
The main takeaway from our work is that
network monitoring queries can be posed in a way that makes them amenable to streaming analytics.
the combination of programmable switches and scalable stream processors can enable network operators to perform flexible and scalable network monitoring in a way that is not possible today.

the design of a scalable system for performing network monitoring queries at scale requires a careful consideration of how the queries should be partitioned, how traffic should be extracted from the switches to the stream processor, how the stream processor should process the traffic, and how the stream processor can communicate with the switches to refine the traffic extraction process.
